title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
description: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to
body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents. Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning. US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show. Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device. The BBC has contacted his representatives.Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court". He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician"."Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday. "We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

schema.headline: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor

title: 400 Mawozo: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
description: The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said.The infamous 40
body: The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said.The infamous 400 Mawozo gang, which is known for kidnappings and intimidation tactics, was targeted in a ground and air attack at a complex on the outskirts of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince.It is El Salvador's first military action on a Haitian target since it deployed more than 2,000 soldiers there last month, as part of a mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran technicians.Haiti has been plagued by gang violence for years, with heavily armed groups controlling large parts of the capital, and beyond.El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced the news on X, external, boasting that most of the gang members fled without trying to fight."We destroyed the house of [gang leader] Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters," he wrote on Tuesday.The post was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex, reportedly in the suburb of Croix-des-Bouquets, the gang's stronghold. As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.Several media outlets have reported that as many as 20 people were killed, however that has not been confirmed by authorities. There has also been no official confirmation of the extent of the damage at the property, with Haitians questioning whether it has been destroyed or just damaged.The Miami Herald reports that the gang's leader, Wilson "Lanmò San Jou" Joseph, was not there at the time.The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the gang's headquarters.Haiti's National Police drone task force was involved in the attack, supported by Salvadoran soldiers, the Miami Herald reports, citing several sources.Posting on X after the strikes, Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé thanked the Salvadoran military's commitment "in the fight against gangs", and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority"."THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!" he added.Some 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were deployed to Haiti last month after four air force technicians were abducted at gunpoint while food shopping in October.El Salvador's right-wing president has vowed to bring the men home alive and warned the gang to release them immediately or face sustained pressure from his military.The four abducted men were working as part of the GSF, made up of troops from several nations, initially led by soldiers from Chad.President Bukele's move to send thousands of Salvadoran troops to Haiti has raised concerns, with critics saying they are not all working within the command structure of the GSF. It has raised questions about the operational legitimacy and legality of their actions in the Caribbean nation.Amnesty International has urged both countries to "ensure all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law".Such concerns do not appear to faze Bukele, however, who continues to directly warn and target the gang leaders.The attack on the supposed gang headquarters seemingly came after a user on X had urged Bukele to attack the complex."Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we'll destroy it," he replied to the post, which has now been taken down, apparently for violating X's rules.The 400 Mawozo gang is the largest criminal organisation in Haiti, and known for kidnappings, extortion, murders and arms trafficking. Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and remains largely under gang control. At least 5,700 people have been killed or injured there by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year alone, the United Nations has said.El Salvador has recorded huge reductions in gang violence under President Bukele as part of a sweeping crackdown, and he has vowed to do the same in Haiti.However, human rights groups have argued that the way he has done it is unlawful, with the open-ended extension of emergency laws, the treatment of detainees in El Salvador's high-security mega-prison and the mass trials of alleged gang members.

schema.headline: 400 Mawozo: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says

title: Asian shops targeted as Eswatini cracks down on illegal foreign businesses
description: Businesses owned by Asian nationals are being closed across Eswatini as the government cracks down on foreign-owned enterprises.The crackdown follows
body: Businesses owned by Asian nationals are being closed across Eswatini as the government cracks down on foreign-owned enterprises.The crackdown follows Parliament's approval of the Citizen Economic Empowerment Act, which seeks to increase ownership and participation by emaSwati, as citizens in the kingdom are known.The legislation follows complaints from local traders that foreign-owned businesses are encroaching on traditional retail markets, increasing competition and threatening livelihoods.South Africa has witnessed more severe enforcement actions, including raids, arrests and the disruption of foreign-run informal businesses, while Kenya has also stepped up action against foreign traders.Its implementation has sparked a heated debate in Parliament, with MPs divided over how quickly foreign businesses owners should be required to leave.Mbabane East MP Welcome Dlamini told Parliament on Tuesday that officials from the trade ministry had already begun enforcing the law by closing Asian-owned shops.Hhohho Regional MP Tanele Magagula called for immediate action, saying "Businesses owned by foreigners in the rural areas must be seized immediately."But Dlamini questioned whether local entrepreneurs were ready to take over the businesses, arguing that foreigner should be given time tio train their successors."Why can't we give the Asians or foreigners at least three years before 'kicking them' out so that emaSwati can learn to run the businesses?" he asked.Magagula rejected the suggestion, questioning why struggling local traders should have to wait while struggling economically."Why must we wait for three years while emaSwati suffer?" she asked.Parliament subsequently agreed that foreign business owners should be given at least 12 months to leave. However, unless the law is formally amended to reflect that timeline, the ministry could continue enforcing its provisions.The closures follow  inspections launched by the trade ministry in August. Some businesses inspected in areas such as Mbabane were found to be fully compliant. However, the inspections also raised concerns about working conditions an administrative practices at foreign-owned enterprises, including complaints by employees over days off, annual leave and overtime. At least one case remains under investigation.Eswatini, a small landlocked kingdom in Southern Africa, faces significant economic hardship, with about 70% of its population living below the poverty line. The government says the new law is intended to expand economic opportunities for citizens, amid concerns that poverty and hunger could fuel further political unrest.The crackdown comes mid growing pressure on foreign-owned businesses elsewhere in the region, particularly in neighbouring South Africa, where anti-immigration campaigns have led to raids, arrests,looting and the disruption of foreign-run informal businesses.On July 30, 2026, the March and March movement intensified its campaign against undocumented immigrants, giving them a deadline to leave. Another protest followed on September 30.The campaigns have been accompanied by violence and attacks on foreign owned businesses.Two Ghanaian and two Nigerian nationals reported killed amid the tensions. Kenya has also stepped up enforcement against foreign traders, bring renewed attention to the treatment of foreign nationals and their businesses across the region.

schema.headline: Asian shops targeted as Eswatini cracks down on illegal foreign businesses

title: US warns Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia
description: The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have
body: The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.US Africa Command deputy head  Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade.He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent.Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have reduced ties with the Western partners and turned to Russia to support their fight against jihadist groups.Russia has expanded its co-operation with Madagascar since the army seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors."We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent," Brennan told reporters in an online briefing."Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.The three Sahel countries had blamed their former Western partners for failing to contain jihadist violence before turning to Moscow.However, Islamist militant attacks have continued despite their closer military ties with Russia.Brennan also raised concerns about security in the Mozambique Channel, which separates Mozambique and Madagascar from mainland Africa and is an important route for international shipping and trade.He said it was vital to prevent militants linked to the Islamist State group in northern Mozambique and other hostile actors from threatening maritime activity.Citing recent piracy-related incidents along the coast, Brennan said they were adapting their tactics, including developing greater maritime capabilities.He said US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish" but urged them to understand the potential risks.Madagascar has not publicly responded to Brennan's comments. However, President Michaël Randrianirina has recently reiterated his support for stronger ties between Russia and African countries.During the Russia-Africa summit last month, Madagascar and Russia signed several co-operation agreements covering defence, tourism and trade.In February, a few months after seizing power, Randrianirina visited to Moscow. It was the first official visit to Russia by a Malagasy leader in nearly 50 years.

schema.headline: US warns Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia

title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
description: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in th
body: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident.Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the RAF base. Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI)."Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year."This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated."On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive."At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason. RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

schema.headline: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says

title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
description: An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol
body: An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill. A majority of the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, for now. In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.However, that calculation could change in January when the Democratic Party assumes control of both chambers of Congress, following its successes in the US midterm elections. For now, Trump's Republican Party remains in control.After Tuesday's vote, the most senior Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, said: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning." The question on which lawmakers were voting on Tuesday was whether or not to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, which is led by Republicans. The alternative would have been to allow the resolution to proceed in the House itself.All Republicans other than Massie voted to refer the resolution to the committee, meaning that the congressman's effort failed in a 211-204 vote. The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress.More than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missed the ballot. Multiple Democrats blamed traffic issues for their absences. Trump celebrated Tuesday's outcome in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED"."Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS. "My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process. The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year. The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail. In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval. The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific  Ocean and Caribbean Sea. At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated". Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations". "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said. He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February. He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.

schema.headline: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now

title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington CemeteryByNardine SaadThe family of former US Presid
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington CemeteryByNardine SaadThe family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery". "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.Figure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed archLast week the project won approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.But US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ruled there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch as litigation plays out.The Kennedy family filed its complaint under a joint lawsuit brought by the state of Virginia and Washington DC seeking to block construction, arguing that the arch will damage "historically significant sightlines" if erected at the gateway of the cemetery. The plaintiffs include seven children of Robert and Ethel Kennedy, as well as their grandson - former Democrat congressman Joe Kennedy - and Ted Kennedy's son Edward Kennedy Jr.It does not include Trump cabinet official Robert F Kennedy Jr, who leads the Department of Health and Human Services.Their motion moves to intervene in two other lawsuits filed by conservationists and veterans seeking to halt the construction. They say the arch would be a "permanent denigration" of the gravesites and that the Kennedy offspring "would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended".The Kennedy family argues the structure "will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family's honor" at the cemetery. The structure would also "fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites", including the memorials of hundreds of thousands of US veterans, the Kennedys said.The complaint said that the National Park Service and Interior Department authorised construction on 5 November 2026 without the necessary congressional approval.The so-called Arc de Trump is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.Last year, he also added his name to the Kennedy Center, a major Washington DC cultural institution named in honour of JFK. Trump's name remained on the facade for six months until the addition was ruled illegal and removed.

schema.headline: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave

title: Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's supporters stage protest
description: Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.Several passenger vehicles were also s
body: Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region. Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere."Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister  Salahuddin Ahmed said."Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist"."She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said."Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

schema.headline: Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's supporters stage protest

title: Tatjana Smith switches allegiance from South Africa to Netherlands
description: South Africa's most decorated Olympian Tatjana Smith was in tears as she announced that she has switched allegiance to the Netherlands.The 29-year-old
body: South Africa's most decorated Olympian Tatjana Smith was in tears as she announced that she has switched allegiance to the Netherlands.The 29-year-old won four Olympic breaststroke medals, including two golds, before retiring after the Paris 2024 Games.She came out of retirement in September and hopes to compete in the 50m breaststroke as the event makes its Olympic debut at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.Smith, whose maiden name was Schoenmaker, wiped away tears as she read a letter addressed to South Africa, saying that "dreams can change as we grow".Smith has dual citizenship because her father is Dutch.She said she has "always been Dutch and South African" and that this is an opportunity to "explore another part of my identity and heritage that I've never experienced through sport".She said it also offers her "greater high-performance support and the potential to build a more sustainable career" because the "financial and practical challenges of swimming were among the reasons my previous career became difficult to sustain".Smith has previously said that financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, contributed to her decision to step away from the sport.Swimming South Africa has been approached for comment.Smith won four world and Commonwealth gold medals between 2018 and 2023.She won gold in the 200m breaststroke and 100m silver at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, before adding 100m gold and 200m silver in 2024."Representing South Africa was a childhood dream come true, and it's a chapter I will always look back on with immense pride and gratitude," she said on social media., external"The people, the memories and everything we achieved together will always be part of me. But dreams can change as we grow."This next chapter is about embracing another part of who I am, falling in love with the journey and discovering what more I'm capable of."I'm excited for what lies ahead, and I truly hope you'll continue to be part of the journey with me."Smith, who said she will continue to live and train in South Africa, is set to represent the Netherlands for the first time at the short course World Championships from 1-6 December.She acknowledged that her switch "may disappoint or break the hearts" of some supporters.The Ministry of Sport, Arts and Culture in South Africa said it was aware of the "problems at Swimming South Africa"."The country was delighted to see her return to the pool, but South Africa does not own her," a statement read."Tatjana's choice belongs to her and it should not be turned into a political weapon."Gayton McKenzie, Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture, said: "Every medal, every record and every anthem she gave us belongs to our history forever. We now have to share her with the Netherlands."

schema.headline: Tatjana Smith switches allegiance from South Africa to Netherlands

title: Spain's king and queen attend memorial service for rail crash victims
description: Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train
body: Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train crash.The accident occurred when one train, travelling at high speed, ploughed into the back of another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line, near the small town of Urda, about 40 miles from Toledo.It was the worst rail tragedy in Spain since 2013. Twenty-eight people remain in hospital."The tragic accident in Urda has left our families, our towns and our society with a pain that is difficult to accept," Archbishop Cerro Chaves told those present.Representatives of those killed carried lit candles to the front of the cathedral and placed them next to the main altar. The first reading of the service was by Ana Benítez, sister of David Benítez, a 38-year-old father-of-two who died.The king and queen were met with applause by bystanders as they entered the cathedral and at the end of the service, after Catholic Mass, they spoke to relatives of the victims.Senior politicians also attended the service, including the leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, and Transport and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo. Cuerpo took on the transport portfolio following the resignation last week of Óscar Puente from the post.

schema.headline: Spain's king and queen attend memorial service for rail crash victims

title: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?
description: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a y
body: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be."You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.That agreement - as well as tariff-free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited."Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one"."We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to qualify for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it"."We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay – capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).This, the federation says, is "a low blow".Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000."Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls."Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits,  "getting them out their comfort zone"."If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"About 200km north, at  Red Valley Farm in Lakeland, general manger Peter Inderbitzen agrees.Workers mainly from Tonga, hired on a Pacific labour scheme, pick bananas there year-round.But Inderbitzen also relies heavily on backpackers, especially at peak avocado season, employing about 25 people for a couple of months each year."It's very short, sharp, get it done, get it out kind of work," he told the BBC. "But without those pickers, the avos stay on the tree."While a few British backpackers were still applying for work, numbers had "completely dropped off" since the rule change, said Inderbitzen, who'd "love" to see British travellers having an incentive to head to the regions."As much as it wasn't perfect, [that programme] was working."Back in Cairns, most of the young Brits the BBC tracks down are on tourist visas - but many want to return for a working holiday.Among them is Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire who has been having way too much fun to keep up to date with what politicians have been discussing."It makes sense for them to want us to do [regional work] again," he says. "I mean I'd rather not do it, but if we have to, it's only three months … it can't be that bad."

schema.headline: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?

title: Real Madrid's Vinicius Jr sends surprise message to Sudanese boy who lost his legs in war
description: Vinícius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs after BBC report sparks appealFigure caption, Watch: Vinícius Jr's surprise messag
body: Vinícius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs after BBC report sparks appealFigure caption, Watch: Vinícius Jr's surprise message to boy who received prosthetic legs after Sudan drone strikeByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspondentReporting fromCairoIn a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.Image source, Vinícius JúniorImage caption, In his video message, Real Madrid star Vinícius Jr invited Zaher to watch a Real Madrid match together The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together."I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer."Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".Image source, Joe McNally/BBCImage caption, Zaher is one of millions of children whose lives have been devastated by Sudan's civil warZaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck."I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection."I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.Image source, Joe McNally/BBCImage caption, Zaher has learned to use his new legs with months of support from doctors and physiotherapists in CairoAfter months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through."He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Khartoum has suffered extensive damage, with many buildings damaged and their contents stolenThe state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine"."I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.Additional reporting by Scarlett Barter and Abdelrahman Abutaleb

title: El Niño in Kenya: 'It can kill us,' says Nairobi resident
description: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of
body: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives."Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid - especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding."I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the front line of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño.Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.But the workers have a huge task on their hands.Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.Nairobi's drainage system has not been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about seven million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely. But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary. However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers."Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come - or how much rain there will be.But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October-December 2026".So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that is because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall."For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean."We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather - including the risk of both floods and drought.The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.

schema.headline: El Niño in Kenya: 'It can kill us,' says Nairobi resident

title: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds
description: One drug comes out top in a large analysis, external of how effective antidepressants are at keeping patients free of symptoms of depression.Escitalop
body: One drug comes out top in a large analysis, external of how effective antidepressants are at keeping patients free of symptoms of depression.Escitalopram performed best at preventing patients from relapsing in a study involving nearly 10,000 people prescribed different medications for up to a year.Two other pills - agomelatine and duloxetine - came next, while prozac (also known as fluoxetine) ranked just below them.Experts stress the findings don't mean that everyone with severe depression should switch to escitalopram, or that other antidepressants aren't any good, because all the drugs can work and each has its pros and cons.  Depression is common, affecting around one in six people in the UK. With the right treatment and support, people can make a good recovery although for some their depression can return.To prevent relapse, doctors already recommend people stay on antidepressants for at least six months after depression ends, and then taper off gradually.The new analysis, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, looked at previous studies comparing the effectiveness of more than a dozen common antidepressants in total.The differences found were modest and experts say longer studies are still needed to find out more. There are many contributing causes to depression and a variety of ways to treat it, including drugs and talking therapies. Experts say patients should discuss what treatment options are best with their doctor.Many medical guidelines recommend SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) antidepressants, like escitalopram, sertraline and fluoxetine or Prozac, as the first drug of choice.These drugs increase seratonin, which is linked to mood. According to the new analysis, compared to Prozac (fluoxetine):people on escitalopram were more likely to see their symptoms improve and stay that way, and less likely to stop taking their medicationagomelatine (an atypical antidepressant) and duloxetine (an SNRI or selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor) also performed wellother medicines, including sertraline, were no better One of the researchers, Prof Eric Ruhé at Radboud University in The Netherlands, said the choice of medication can vary for each individual."Nevertheless, our study can help inform the decisions that prescribers and patients make together: if you start an antidepressant, choose one that not only helps you to get well, but also keeps you well."Dr Sameer Jauhar, an expert at Imperial College London, said while the research provided useful information, "it cannot tell us which antidepressant will work best for an individual patient.""I would not interpret these findings as a reason for someone who is responding well to their current antidepressant to change treatment," he added.Prof Allan Young from the Royal College of Psychiatrists said: "While some medicines appear to have a small advantage over others for longer-term outcomes, the differences are modest and are unlikely to outweigh individual factors such as side effects, previous response and patient preference when deciding on treatment."Like all medicines, escitalopram can cause side effects, including sleep problems, constipation and weight gain, although not everyone experiences them.The NHS says, external if escitalopram or a similar SSRI is ineffective or not suitable, doctors may suggest a different type of antidepressant, such as an SNRI.Older tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, are now less commonly prescribed.The mental health charity Mind says people need access to clear information about the potential benefits and side effects of antidepressants as well as other forms of support, including talking therapies and mindfulness."It's common for people to need to try more than one medication before they find the right treatment that works for them. And what works may change over time," the charity said.Mind's website, external has information to help compare different antidepressants.

schema.headline: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds

title: Inside devastated front-line city of Slovyansk that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
description: Figure caption, Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting devastated front-line cityByJonathan Beale Defence correspondentReporting fro
body: Figure caption, Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting devastated front-line cityByJonathan Beale Defence correspondentReporting fromSlovyansk, eastern UkraineThe dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start."If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air. They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.Image source, BBC/Moose CampbellImage caption, Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardmentOnce inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun – a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.Abandoned vehicles litter the streets – recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up – making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy – to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas – like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas – made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion – with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.Image source, BBC/Moose CampbellImage caption, Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stayBefore the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born."I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.  "It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown"."I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.Image source, BBC/Moose CampbellImage caption, Commander Oleksandr of the Peaky Blinders special forces unit says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in useWe first met the Omega National Guard Special Forces drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show – "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day – he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby."I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line."We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far."I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".Image source, EPAImage caption, The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensifyThe next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.  "Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.Additional reporting by Rebecca Hartmann, Volodymyr Lozhko and Moose Campbell.

schema.headline: Inside devastated front-line city of Slovyansk that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
